positions.playedPrefix: e4

existingAccepted.title: Meet Space With a Central Policy
existingAccepted.question: What central commitment can White make before Black has chosen a defensive setup?
existingAccepted.takeaway: White claims space and opens lines for the queen and king's bishop. Black's problem is not an immediate threat, but White's ability to add another central pawn and develop behind it. Our repertoire accepts that space initially, then challenges it with supported pawn contact rather than trying to prevent every white advance.
existingAccepted.intent: The pawn controls d5 and f5, making White's central presence felt immediately. It also releases the bishop on f1. Black needs a response that challenges this space while leaving a workable development scheme; simply matching White's pawn moves is not the only way to do that.
existingAccepted.plan: The repertoire answers with ...c6 and meets d4 with ...d5. White can then advance, defend, or exchange the e-pawn. This line follows the exchange, but Black should first understand the common central challenge: the later bishop and knight placements depend on which pawn structure White chooses.
existingAccepted.tactic: After the planned ...c6 and ...d5, exd5 can be answered by a pawn recapture. That is the concrete mechanism behind Black's setup, not an immediate threat after e4. Before committing to a central challenge, identify both the opponent's possible capture and your intended recapturing piece.
existingAccepted.theme: White starts by claiming space; Black will answer by questioning its support. The later exchanges and open-file play grow from that central policy rather than from a permanently defensive formation.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied 1.d4 continuation builds a queen's-pawn center with c4 and ...e6. That is a different initial problem. Here e4 releases the king's bishop immediately and allows Black to choose the specific ...c6 and ...d5 framework studied in this line.

positions.playedPrefix: e4 c6

existingAccepted.title: Prepare Contact Before Developing Pieces
existingAccepted.question: How should Black balance challenging White's space with preserving flexible piece development?
existingAccepted.takeaway: Black prepares ...d5 with a pawn that can recapture there. This is an investment, not a developing move or an immediate attack on e4. Its value is that the coming central confrontation need not expose the queen, while the e-pawn remains at home and the c8 bishop's eventual route stays undecided.
existingAccepted.intent: The c-pawn supports d5 without occupying the c8 bishop's diagonal. There is a development cost: c6 is temporarily unavailable to the b8 knight. Black therefore needs to use the prepared central challenge, rather than spend further moves building a shelter without contesting White's space.
existingAccepted.plan: Meet the line's d4 with ...d5, then adapt to White's response. The supplied Nc3 continuation instead reaches ...dxe4 and ...Bf5. That bishop placement belongs to a particular structure; it is not a commitment made by ...c6 itself. Our Exchange line will require a different development sequence.
existingAccepted.tactic: The intended recapture matters after ...d5 and exd5: ...cxd5 restores material while keeping the queen out of attack. Until Black actually plays ...d5, however, e4 is not challenged. White is free to reinforce the center or develop rather than react to an imagined immediate threat.
existingAccepted.theme: Black exchanges a little development time for a reliable central mechanism. In this line, using that mechanism will also clear c6 for a knight and leave the c-file available for later rook activity.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied ...c5 continuation challenges White through a different pawn structure, followed by ...Nc6 and ...d6. Our ...c6 instead supports ...d5. The useful comparison is the intended pawn contact and resulting development, not a claim that one opening name guarantees greater solidity.

positions.playedPrefix: e4 c6 d4

existingAccepted.title: White Builds the Full Pawn Center
existingAccepted.question: How can White use Black's preparatory tempo to strengthen the central position?
existingAccepted.takeaway: White establishes two central pawns and gives both bishops routes into play. This is a substantial use of the first-move initiative, not an overextension that Black can automatically punish. Black should nevertheless remain consistent: the previous move prepared a supported central challenge, and White's larger center makes carrying out that challenge more relevant.
existingAccepted.intent: The d-pawn controls c5 and e5, complementing the e-pawn's influence over d5 and f5. White has gained space without developing a piece yet. Black can contest the center before that space becomes the base for a fully coordinated army.
existingAccepted.plan: Continue with ...d5. White can then retain space through e5 or exchange on d5, as in our line. In the supplied ...d6 alternative, White keeps both pawns while developing Nf3 and Nbd2. That illustrates the difference between immediately challenging a center and preparing to contain it.
existingAccepted.tactic: After ...d5, White's e-pawn will be attacked even though White has two pawns in the center. Side-by-side pawns do not protect each other. Capturing on d5 is possible, but the c6 pawn supplies Black's recapture, so the contact is not an offer of a free pawn.
existingAccepted.theme: The position presents the problem Black's first move anticipated. Rather than retreating from White's space, Black will use the prepared support to make White choose the central structure.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied 2.Nc3 can also support a broad center, but ...d5 3.d4 ...dxe4 leads to a knight recapture. Playing d4 first leaves that knight uncommitted and keeps the Exchange option available without first choosing its development square.

positions.playedPrefix: e4 c6 d4 d5

existingAccepted.title: Turn Preparation Into Central Contact
existingAccepted.question: White has occupied the center with two pawns; how should Black make the previous tempo count?
existingAccepted.takeaway: Black attacks e4 and makes White choose how to handle the center. The c6 pawn provides a natural recapture if White exchanges, so the challenge does not depend on early queen activity. Black also opens a route for the c8 bishop, although its best destination still depends on White's reply.
existingAccepted.intent: The new pawn attacks e4 and controls c4, supported by both c6 and the queen. Black has established contact, not an advantage. White retains several sound ways to define the structure, and Black must recognize the different development tasks those choices create.
existingAccepted.plan: Answer this line's exd5 with ...cxd5. Against e5, the supplied branch instead develops ...Bf5 before ...e6; against Nc3 or Nd2, the candidates exchange on e4. Learn these as different structural responses rather than assuming every Caro–Kann position calls for the same bishop maneuver.
existingAccepted.tactic: After exd5, Black can legally recapture with either pawn or queen. Compare what White can attack next: ...cxd5 retains a central pawn, whereas an exposed queen can become a target for developing moves. The identity of the recapturing piece determines more than material balance.
existingAccepted.theme: Black's opening moves now form a complete idea: prepare the confrontation, then create it. White's next decision will select the Exchange structure and replace general opening principles with more specific plans.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied ...d6 setup continues with ...Nf6 and ...g6, containing rather than immediately challenging White's center. It is a different plan, but makes less direct use of c6's support and gives White more time with both central pawns intact.

positions.playedPrefix: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5

existingAccepted.title: White Chooses Clarity Over Space
existingAccepted.question: How can White resolve the central tension without committing to a closed pawn chain?
existingAccepted.takeaway: White exchanges the e-pawn for Black's original d-pawn. After the expected recapture, fewer pawns will occupy the center and White can develop the king's bishop actively. This is not surrendering the initiative. White is choosing a contest of development and piece coordination instead of trying to maintain a broad pawn center.
existingAccepted.intent: The capture removes the tension between e4 and d5. White temporarily has two pawns on the d-file, but the advanced pawn is available for recapture. Judge the lasting structure after Black's reply, not by treating this intermediate arrangement as a permanent weakness.
existingAccepted.plan: Restore material with ...cxd5 and then respond to White's setup. Bd3 and c3 will establish the restrained Exchange formation used here. The supplied candidates also include c4 after the recapture, which challenges d5 immediately and changes the development problem into a Panov-type central contest.
existingAccepted.tactic: The supplied ...Qxd5 4.c4 continuation shows why the recapture matters: White attacks the queen while increasing central influence. Black need not accept that loss of time. The pawn recapture restores material without presenting the queen as a target for White's next advance.
existingAccepted.theme: White has declined the Advance structure. Black's coming activity will revolve around development and a possible ...e5 challenge, not around undermining a white pawn chain that no longer exists.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied 3.e5 continuation closes the center and leads to ...Bf5, ...e6, and ...c5. Exd5 removes that chain instead. Plans for attacking an Advance center cannot be transferred unchanged to a position where White's e-pawn has been exchanged.

positions.playedPrefix: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5

existingAccepted.title: Recapture Without Exposing the Queen
existingAccepted.question: How can Black restore material while retaining a central foothold and useful development options?
existingAccepted.takeaway: The c-pawn recaptures and becomes Black's pawn on d5. Material is restored, c6 becomes available to the knight, and the queen stays out of White's developing attacks. The opposing d-pawns now block one another. Black can develop around that contact while considering when the remaining e-pawn should challenge White's center.
existingAccepted.intent: Black has a half-open c-file and White a half-open e-file. The d5 pawn is not isolated yet, because Black still has an e-pawn. This asymmetry matters: the central pawns face each other, but the two sides do not have identical pawn structures or identical future breaks.
existingAccepted.plan: After Bd3, develop ...Nc6 with pressure on d4 and support for ...e5. White's c3 reinforcement produces our main structure. The supplied c4 alternative attacks d5 immediately, so Black would need to reassess the central tension rather than mechanically repeat the same quiet development plan.
existingAccepted.tactic: The supplied ...Qa5+ detour allows Qd2, ...Qxd5, and Nc3 with an attack on the queen. A check has not prevented White from gaining development tempi. The played recapture avoids that sequence and preserves the queen's support of d5 from its original square.
existingAccepted.theme: The opening preparation has produced more than a safe recapture. It has also released a knight square and created a half-open file, benefits that will reappear in Black's later piece activity.
existingAccepted.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Qxd5 is legal, but c4 attacks the queen and forces another decision about her placement. ...cxd5 instead makes a pawn the central occupant. It restores material while keeping future development focused on minor pieces rather than queen relocation.
